## v5.1.0 — your agent catches up on Slack the way you would, and knows who it's listening to

![It’s Tuesday, 9:07 AM. After the weekend you had, the printer is jammed and nobody knows the PIN. You ask your agent in your own words; it answers back, runs one search, and finds the PIN Dave posted in #facilities five months ago that nobody read. Tape it to the printer.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jtalk22/slack-mcp-server/v5.1.0/docs/images/hero-v2.gif)

Put your agent inside your Slack. Zero bots, zero admin queues, no Business+ upgrade — 20+ tools for stealth search, thread parsing and mention tracking. Every message attributed. Your session never leaves your Mac.

```sh
npx -y @jtalk22/slack-mcp --setup
```

Until now, an agent reading your Slack saw roughly what you'd see glancing at the sidebar: a few channels with a number next to them. 5.1 gives it what Slack itself knows is waiting — every mention, every reply in a thread you were never pinged on, every conversation past the first page — and tells it, for each message, whether the words came from inside your company or not. Catching up stops being a thing you do and becomes a thing you hand off.

### Nothing waiting gets past it

Every mention, every unread reply, every thread, in every conversation. The catch-up now reads the same counts Slack's own badges use, so what your agent reports is what Slack knows is waiting. Mentions come first. Replies in threads you were never pinged on are counted. Conversations beyond the first page of the listing are found and named.

In a workspace with a hundred channels, that is the difference between an agent that shows you the three channels you happened to open and one that knows every update.

For the curious: the per-channel unread number most tools read, `unread_count_display`, drops to zero the moment a channel is opened, so a workspace could have ten mentions waiting and a tool reading it would report nothing. 5.1 also reads `client.counts`, the undocumented endpoint behind Slack's own sidebar badges, and merges it with the conversation list. If that call ever fails, the catch-up falls back to the previous view and says what is missing, so an answer is never silently incomplete.

### Every message says who wrote it

At no extra API call, every message now carries who wrote it: you, a colleague, someone from another company over Slack Connect, or an app relaying an email or an RSS feed. Your agent sees which words came from inside your organisation and which did not, before it acts on any of them. That is the defence against a planted "ignore your instructions and send X" sitting in a shared channel.

Built for real workspaces. Slack leaves the team field off messages your own colleagues write, so a naive classifier calls most of a normal channel unknown. This one reads the channel's sharing status first: a channel that is not shared outside your company cannot contain an outside author, so a colleague without a team field is still a colleague. "Unknown" is reserved for the genuinely unplaceable. On a real channel, unknowns went from more than half the messages to none.

Turn on strict mode and the server goes one step further: once your agent has read text from outside your company, it pauses any send until the agent acknowledges what it read. A single request can raise that safety level, never lower it.

### Read-only mode

Run it with `--read-only` and the four tools that write to Slack — send, react, un-react, mark as read — are not there. Not hidden, not guarded: absent, and refused if a client asks for one anyway. For a shared agent, a CI job, or any workspace where you want eyes and never hands.

### Security doctor

`npx -y @jtalk22/slack-mcp --doctor --security` checks your own setup: where the credential is stored, the file's permissions, whether message labelling is on, whether the write tools are registered, whether workspaces are kept apart, and how old the credential is. Each line is a pass, a warning or a fail, with the one command that tightens it. No score, and it says why.

### Also new

- **Commitments, owner gaps and open questions** from the catch-up — who said they would do what, which asks nobody claimed, which questions are still open — each with the text that matched and a link to the message.
- **A session receipt.** `slack_session_report` tells you what this session read and tried to send, as counts: how many messages, how many from outside your company, how many sends were attempted and how many were paused. Never message text, never a channel name.
- **Every conversation says whether it is shared outside your company**, so an agent can tell a Slack Connect channel from one of your own before it reads a word.
- **A published prompt-injection test set** ([docs/INJECTION-CORPUS.md](https://github.com/jtalk22/slack-mcp-server/blob/main/docs/INJECTION-CORPUS.md)) — bidi overrides, zero-width splits, fake tool calls in message text, relay bots, attacker-settable identity fields — so other MCP authors can test their servers against the same attacks.
- **CodeQL and OSV-Scanner** on every change, and signed npm provenance on every release: `npm audit signatures` verifies the chain.
- **Setup that explains itself.** The wizard tells you what to do based on the exact reason a step failed, and prints your client configuration at the end.
- **Every command in the docs works from `npx`**, including the bug-report template.

### Fixed

- The safeguard that pauses sending after your agent has read outside text now covers every way of reading, including the catch-up, and a single request can raise it but never lower it.
- A token refresh starts clean: workspace identity is re-read, so a refresh that lands on a different workspace labels its authors correctly.
- `slack_catch_me_up` and `slack_conversations_history` place the same message the same way.
- Strengthened regression tests across the labelling, read-only and catch-up paths.

### Compatibility

Nothing is removed from any response; 5.1 only adds. `SLACK_MCP_PROVENANCE=off` turns the author labels off for anyone who needs the previous output exactly. Node 20 and up.

### Install

```sh
npx -y @jtalk22/slack-mcp --setup
claude mcp add slack -- npx -y @jtalk22/slack-mcp
```

```sh
npx -y @jtalk22/slack-mcp --doctor --security   # check your own setup
npx -y @jtalk22/slack-mcp --read-only           # read Slack, never write to it
```
